# Day 1 — Consolidation {#sec-consolidation}

**20 minutes · plenary**

## Say it in one sentence

Without notes, write the single sentence you would say to a ward manager who
asks what your model does. It must contain a number, the units of that number,
and the condition under which the number holds.

A sentence that meets the bar:

> On patients like the ones we trained on, it predicts length of stay to within
> about three days on average — roughly a quarter of the error you would make by
> guessing the average — and we have no evidence it holds if the case-mix or the
> discharge pathway changes.

Count how many of the three elements your own sentence has.

## Self-assessment

Tick honestly. Anything unticked is what to review before Day 2.

- [ ] I can write a filter, a group-level summary and a linear fit in **both** languages.
- [ ] I can name the five pipeline steps and what each protects against.
- [ ] I can explain why a score computed on training rows is not evidence.
- [ ] I compared my model against a baseline and can state the ratio.
- [ ] I can define covariate shift and concept shift without using the word "distribution" twice.
- [ ] I can say which of the two is detectable without outcomes.
- [ ] I can state the assumption my model's accuracy depends on, in words.

## Five questions

Answer in a sentence each. These are the form the written assessment takes.

1. Your test MAE is 3 days and your baseline MAE is 13 days. A colleague says
   the model is "77% accurate". What is wrong with that sentence?
2. You split 80/20 and get a test MAE of 3.0. Your colleague splits 80/20 on the
   same data and gets 3.7. Who made the mistake?
3. A model is fitted on 2019 admissions and used in 2021. Age and severity at
   admission look exactly as they did in 2019, but the model's errors have
   doubled. What kind of shift is this, and what must have been available to you
   in order to notice?
4. Give one reason a model might predict length of stay well using a variable
   that would be useless to act on.
5. You are handed a model with a test MAE better than anything you can
   reproduce. What two things do you ask for before believing it?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) "Accurate" has no meaning for a continuous outcome and 77% is a
ratio of two errors, not a proportion of correct predictions; the defensible
phrasing is "its average error is about a quarter of the baseline's". (2)
Neither. A single split is a noisy estimate; the spread they measured in
Stretch 2 is 0.7 days wide, so 3.0 and 3.7 are the same result. This question
is the one that most reliably separates students who did the stretch task.
(3) Concept shift with no covariate shift; noticing it required *outcomes* —
observed lengths of stay — because nothing in the inputs changed. (4) Prediction
exploits association, intervention requires causation: a variable can be a
marker of the process that drives the outcome (e.g. number of prior referrals)
without being a lever on it. (5) The split — was the test set held out before
any fitting, and was it used once — and the baseline. Anyone who asks for the
code rather than those two has not got the point of today.

**Rubric** (if the day is assessed, 20 marks):

| | Marks |
|---|---|
| Pipeline runs end to end on the birth-weight data, correct split, evaluated once | 6 |
| Baseline computed and the comparison stated as a ratio | 3 |
| Residual plot with a statement about *whose* predictions are worst | 3 |
| Correct classification of A, B and C | 3 |
| Evidence named for each classification (distributions for case-mix, refitted coefficients for the relationship) | 3 |
| One-sentence claim containing a number, its units and its condition | 2 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[80,20]"}

Mark the evidence, not the classification: a student who reasons from refitted
coefficients and mislabels one extract has understood more than one who guessed
all three from the MAE column.
:::
:::

## What carries into Day 2

Three loose ends were left deliberately, and each opens the next session.

1. **One split is a noisy estimate.** The fix is resampling — cross-validation,
   repeated splits, the bootstrap.
2. **MAE was chosen for us.** It treats a 1-day error and a 30-day error as
   proportionally equal, which is a clinical assumption nobody checked.
3. **The outcome is implausible.** Real length of stay is right-skewed with a
   median of a few days. `data/los_data_skewed.csv` is waiting for the session
   where that matters.

## Further reading

Two papers that make today's lesson concrete at the scale of a health system.
Futoma and colleagues argue that generalisability as usually claimed is a myth
and that validation belongs in the setting of use [@futoma2020]. Wynants and
colleagues appraised every covid-19 prediction model published in the first
months of the pandemic and found almost all of them at high risk of bias,
mostly for reasons you met today — no baseline, no genuine held-out
evaluation, no account of who the patients were [@wynants2020]. TRIPOD+AI
[@collins2024] is the reporting standard you will be held to; skim the
checklist now and notice how much of it is about the split.
